INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION AND THE
GENEVA. AWARD.

Ix my two preceding articles I sought to
point out some of the evils arising from stand-
ing armies, more especially their costliness to
the nation and the danger to its liberties
occasioned by their existence. I now wish to
offer a few remarks as to the necessity of adopt-
ing International Arbitration as a means of
freeing ourselves from these evils.
The noble idea of preserving friendliness
amongst various States or nations by a peace-
able arrangement of what mutually concerns
them ia by no means new, Upon it was
founded the old Amphictyonic Council, and
the same idea is solidly embodied in Christian
thought, although practically excluded from
Christian action. This ignoring of Christian
duty so glaring, and at the same time so shock-
ing and atrocious, has, in the annals of
Europe, been punished with an almost destruo
tive severity—without finding adequate cor-
rection. A project, having also for its object
the abolition of war, was devised by that truly
. philanthropic) and illustrious man HENRY
IV., of France, and was submitted by him to
Queen ELIZA.BETII, of England, but was lost to
the world by his cruel and untimely death.
. It is a happy circumstance that the same
thought in another:shape should have sought
so recently to work itself into life at Genova;
and if the Alabama Arbitration can be estab-
lished as a precedent for settling the quarrels
of nations, it will in all future times be re-
garded by men as the event—in merely human
affairs—through whioli the largest amount of
good has come to the world.
The Geneva award will meet with some
amount of censure in England, because on
certain points it is not in accord with national
vanity, public prejudice, and individual
interest. But one of the first and principa
thoughts to be taken into men's minds in con-
nection with the decisions of arbitration, is
that they cannot possibly give satisfaction to
everybody—that they always must give
dissatisfaction to some of the parties con-
cerned. It should not be forgotten, more-
over, that in arbitration no loss of
honour can attach to an adverse decision,
Provided there be no evil design in
seeking for arbitration, and the nation or
individual that would ask for an adjudication
conscious of a bad cause would be as con-
spicuous for wickedness as for folly. However
much, therefore, a few Englishmen may con-
demn certain points in the Geneva award, the
fact must not be overlooked that our honour as

and kings, if not sheathed, would speedily be
turned upon themselves—thus constituting
them an expiatory sacrifice for past sin, and a
promise of peace to the world for all time to
come.

It has often been urged that international
arbitration now exists, inasmuch as before
any war is entered on, diplomacy is active to
avert it. It may be replied, how-
ever, that diplomacy is as often active
to provoke war, that the agents of
emperors and kings only take into account
the interests, passions, and ambitions of their
masters, whilst the tribunal of nations, acting
on behalf of peoples, and bringing to bear, on
all discussions, the considerations of their
collective interests, backed up by the 'masses
interested in every way in the preservation of
peace, would soon cause kingly ambitions to
kick the beam.
It is undeniable that national murder is
falling into disfavour, that thoughts of amity
and peace grow daily stronger in men's
minds, and it is a melancholy fact that the
losses of war are pressing painfully, almost
destructively, on the industrial energies of
nations. People are beginning to see that
the Millions wasted in destructive wars, the
taxes paid annually as interest on debts in-
curred in these wars, which, together with the
charges for maintaining our standing army,
amount, in this country alone, to more titan
one thousand millions of pounds sterling every
twenty years, could he better used in making
roads, building bridges, opening mines, drain-
ing marshes, exploring distant regions, culti-
vating commercial enterprise, spreading know-
ledge, and extending the blessings of civiliza-
tion to every corner of the globe.
Let the working men of England lead the
way in exalting this great and salutary prin-
ciple of arbitration. In their trades disputes,
in all differences of interest, even of anger,
but above all, in regard to the destructive and
sanguinary wars of monarchs, lot arbitration
be called for and insisted On, and time, co-
operating with wisdom, humanity, and justtee,
will give a triumphant and happy issue to
their efforts. We Englishmen are here in
our inviolable island, girt in by the sea, free
from fear of outside attack. Let us, therefore,
who are above all suspicion of fear, begin to
preach this great gospel of peace, of goodwill
amongst men, not as dreamers, not as utopian
fanatics, but as practical men of common
sense, inert who have discovered and applied
the mighty, the inexhaustible resources of in-
dustry; and who know that by peaceably
pursuing our various callings we can make
every life happy, and every home comfort.
able and secure.

THE able article by Fanntitic HARRISON in
the recent issue of the _Fortnightly Beview
calls for special attention. It is characterised
by the writer's usual consummate ability, and
deals with facts of the highest interest to all
who have in any way made the relations of
capital and labour a study, or who, whilst con-
sidering these, have felt anxious as to the best
method for bringing about their find recon-
ciliation.

Mr. IlakssEY's book is not more striking by
the importance of its facts,than by the fair and
manly spirit in. which it is written. Whilst
this comment on it by Mr. HARRISON gives so
clear an understanding of its meaning in
relation to the industry of the country, and
the future condition of the worker, in connec-
tion with his work, that where we agree with
him we feel an unwonted confidence as the
result of that agreement; and where we differ
wo are conscious how necessary it is that we
should examine with the utmost care and self-
distrust the grounds of our difference..

Mr. Iliniusori fully recognizes the trust-
worthiness of his facts; he knows that with
Mr. BaAMEY'S book in his hand, on the ground
of fact, he is unassailable, arid, therefore, with
an admirable skill and an irresistible power
he utterly demolishes the flimsy structures of
false statement which the employ.:.ls, the sham
economists, the Times, and the ordinary gang
of poor scribblers who follow its lead have
been building up for many years. After read-
ing the article in the Fortaiyhtly, nobody can
believe that trades unions have a tendency to
drive capital or trade out of the country—that
they have driven shipbuilding from the
Thames, that they have unnaturally advanced
the price of labour in proportion to the amount
of work done, or, in fact, produced any one of
the evils charged against them by their
enemies. If Mr. BRASSEY'S book anti Mr.
lautusox's article on it do not settle the
question between the trades unionists and the

nothing left but to wait patiently the result

countries, a succession of efforts fruitful of
good, but separated by saddening intervals of
blindness and barbarism : the succession of
human heroes not being complete enough to
' keep the world in the glorious paths trodden
by the feet of really great men—the Sage,
who embodies in his thought or exemplifies
by his act the highest knowledge developed by
the most recent experience, is surrounded by
multitudes whose practices are regulated
in a great measure by past ignorance. The
great individual is circumscribed and limited
by the briefness of his existence, the greatest
men, in a certain sense, only aid the world for
a time; the unbreken succession of numbers
alone can add perpetuity to greatness in human
work. Numbers, in the spirit of co-operation,
can attain ends which single individuals could

can execute undertakings which would have
baffled the mightiest of earth's old giants.
And the labours of vast 'associations resting
with their 'whole weight on true principles,

The power of the single great man is un-

at his highest result by many hands labouring
as one, and by many harmonised interests
operating in one direction. Co-operation may
therefore be truly regarded not only as a great
material gain to the world, but as a true disci-
pline in humanity. And seeing what it has
already done, and what it aims at accomplish-
ing, it is to be regretted that any honest
thinker should pelt it with ugly epithets.

but moderate labour. Such have been the im-
provements in machinery, in tools, and in the
division of labour that a workman in almost
every department of industry can at present
produce as much in one hour as he could have
done one hundred years ago in four. There
is, therefore, not the slightest excuse for the
master employers striving to keep up long
hours of labour under the pretence of getting
the full profit of their machinery, as if the
skilled workman of England is not the most
valuable article of our machinery and the
article upon which chiefly depends our
immense national wealth and our indua-
trial superiority over every nation in the
world.

I maintain that no workman should be era-
ployed longer than is good for his health. If
this be done, the labourer becomes prematurely
old and deerepid. Besides, even during hia
youth he is prevented from intellectual enjoy-
ment; for when a man is overworked, when
he leaves off he has no taste or pleasure in
anything but stimulants, such as smoking
and drinking. The first question, then, is---
What should be the number of the hours of
labour? That is a question which should be
determined by a council of medical man, vim,
how many hours can a man of average
strength work without injury to his health?
I am convinced if this question was put to a
medical board the answer would be eight hours
a day at the most. I was an employer 4:4
labour myself for a number of years, both as
a coal master and a farmer, and from
my experience and observation I kilo!
that every labourer who attempts, or le
driven to work more than this, is sill.°
to shorten his life, or, at least, t°
bring on rheumatism, or other complaints
which render old age a misery. I have talked
to labourers as to the proper duration of work,
and the result to which We came was this.. 4.
labourer should commence work at meat
o'clock, after having breakfasted half an hour
before. He should work till twelve (four

hours) and then leave off for an hour, dorillg,
which time he would lunch. At one he W 0
recommence his labour and work until 08
(four hours more). After fire, he would waoh

himself, go home to his family, or his working
man's club if he was a batchelor, and dine
like a gentleman, having all the evening to
himself to read or otherwise amuse himself.
Such h the manner in which I maintain the
labourer, both agricultural and mechanical,
should live and work. Of course this mode of
life could not always be preserved. In harvest
time, for instance, there would require to
be additional hours of toil. But such spirts of
additional labour, carried on for a short time,
could do no injury, if it was accompanied by
a moderate addition of food and of beer.

The question as to the amount of wages can
now be settled by any fixed rules. This, must
he determined by the amount of demand and
supply of capital and labour, and this is
regulated by constantly varying circumstances.
But the duration of the daily work might
be settled, not invariably, but as a general
rule. Much might be done in this respect by
Government—by the men in the dookyards,
the arsenals, and other public works not being
kept employed more than eight hours a day.
This would give a tone to the whole industrial
operations in the country, and would induce
nail owners and other private capitalists tq
follow the example of Government and
limit their operations to eight hours a day.
I would even go further than this. I see no
reason why an Act of Parliament should
not be passed regulating the duration of
labour, and prescribing the hours at which
every factory should be opened and shut. Of
course, such an Act could not be imperative
in every case. There would be power 'given
to the authorities to relax it upon cause,
shown. Ido not see the slightest reason, I re-
peat, why such an Act of Parliament should
not be passed. The capitalists,- no doubt,
would say that it interfered with the liberty
of action. So said the American planters when
a fine was proposed to prevent them from
walloping their own niggers. The British
Parliament has passed an Act to fix the hours
of opening and shutting public-houses. Why,
I ask, should not the same be done with regard
to factories and workshops? I am convinced
I repeat, that long hours of toil—excessive
labour in short-4s infinitely more conducive
to drinking than the leaving open the public
houses to a late hour of the night. If we had
a House of Commons where the rights of
labour were properly represented—that is to
say by members selected from among the
working classes themselves on account of their
intellectual superiority—a Bill such as I have
sketched would soon he introduced.

JAMES ATTOU.N.

THE TLILES ON SOCIAL SCIENCE.

IT is evident from the proceedings of the
gentlemen who have met together at Plymouth
to discuss what they call Social Science, that
they have yet to learn what the science is
which they undertake to promote. The Times
is desirous to instruct them, but it requires
instruction quite as much as they do. It tells
us that it is "disposed to think that a really
practical philosopher, looking upon human
nature as something which he had to inter-
pret and not to create, would regard the
existing forms of civilization as the only guides
he could obtain to what was possible and
desirable." And it is of opinion that "existing
institutions are, as a matter of fact, the pro-
duct of human nature working untrammeled,
and developing its organization from simple
elements." The 7imeB is quite mistaken.
Existing institutions, including the Times it-
self, are the products of the working of human
nature trammeled by ignorance and erroneous
ideas in reference to the causes of evil and of
good to man, in the formation of character, in
the production and distribution of wealth, and
in the arrangements, and institutions, and
general proceedings of societies. The existing
forms of what is called civilization, instead of
being the only guides to what is possible and
desirable, are merely the guides to what alone
is possible, and what is inevitable, while so-
ciety is ignorant of these causes; just as the
old modes of travelling were guides to what
was possible when men were ignorant of rail-
ways and steamships. But existing institu-
tions are no more guides to what will be
possible and what will be inevitable when
mu hays acquired the knowledge of those

causes, and the moral development which this
icnowledge alone can enable them to acquire,
than the old roads and ships were guides to
What gubsequently became " practicable and
has been realized in travelling.
•Our present modes of education, by which
All are caused to acquire the very defective
Intellectual and moral character which is now
Universal, are products of the working of

human nature vihile it is trammeled by igno-
rance and 'erroneous ideas in reference to the
Causes of evil and of good in the formation of
character, dm Are they the only guides
Which man can obtain as to what is possible
and desirable in education?

Our present modes of producing and dis-
tributing wealth, which are the cause of so
much injustice, and poverty, and misery,
especially to the working classes, and of so
much moral and physical evil to all, are the
products of the working of human nature
trammeled by ignorance and erroneous ideas in
reference to the production and clistributiou of
wealth, and by the very defective moral
development of all classes. Are they the only
guides which we can obtain as to what is
possible and desirable in the production and
distribution of wealth?

And the same may be said, and the same
question .may be asked, with respect to the
arrangements, and institutions, and general
practices of the existing system".
It is very sad, when society is in the terrible
plight in which it is, and when it is in such
urgent need of enlightenmerit, that its most
prominent instructors should have little else
than what is practically, useless, and worse to
deal out to it upon these vitally important
subjects. But it is the product of the working
of human nature while trammeled by ignor-
ance and error. Happily, however, this is not
the only guidance which is now to be obtained
as to what is practicable and desirable. I need
not extend these remarks at present. Any-
one who wishes to know more on this subject
may obtain for a penny a little tract of eight
pages, on "The Coming Revolution" (advertised
on page 8), which will give him further infor-
mation. HENRY TRAVIS.

THE LATE BUILDERS' STRIKE.

THE Joni-ans.—On Saturday evening the dele-
gation from the London carpenters and joiners en-
trusted with the carrying out of the recent
movement and strike for the "nine hours and
ninepence was virtually dissolved. The last
act of the °antral committee was to declare that
they looked upon the recent compromise berween
the masters' committee and their deputation, not
as a final settlement of the claims put forth in
their memorial, but more in the nature of an
armistice, leaving the trade free to renew its
efforts in favour of the full terms of the memorial
on the first favourable opportunity. The secre-
tary has been instructed to call together a new
delegation from all societies, shops, and jobs,
having for its object the adoption of measures to
enforce compliance with the terms of the new
agreement in those firms—about forty in number
—who continue working on the old system of 66i
hours at Bd. per hour; the extension of the union
organization throughout London; and the laying
down a plan of action for renewing the movement
to obtain the 51 hours at Dd. an hour in the spring
oftnext year, should the state of business justify
such action being taken.
-Tun Masorrs.—A serious complication has
arisen between; the Master Builders' Association
and the Masons' Society. It appears that, in the
aireement made between the co mmittee of
masters and the masons' deputation, they were to
leave off work at twelve o'clock on Saturdays all
the year round, but the agreements entered into
with the other trades specify one o'clock as the
leaving off hour on Saturdays during the winter
months. The masons' deputation made no dis-
tinct arrangement with the masters' committee as
to paym-nt for overtime, it having been a
recognized ustorn in the trade that all overtime
worked by masons beyond the regular working
hours each day was paid for at the rate of time
and a half for every hour up till ten p.m., and
double time up to six o'clock a.m. The agree-
ments made with the carpenters and the other
trades include arrangements for overtime, and its
payment at the rate of H. extra for the first hour
after five p.m.; at the rate of 2d. per hour extra
for the next two hours; and time and a half after-
wards. It will thus be seen that the payment for
overtime to be made to the other trades is con-
siderably less than the amount now received by
the masons. The masters have called upon the
masons to accept these terms as regards the hour
for leaving off on Saturday and overtime payment,
and to modify their agreement accordingly. This
the masons' committee ;have refused to do, and
have further informed the Masters that any
attempt on their part to tamper with the terms of
the agreement, or to alter the recognized paymen
for overtime received by the masons, would be
resisted by the whole power of the society.

TILE PA/NTEILE.-011 Monday a mooting was

.con-

gated that Mr. Dines, one of the members of the

advice. The speaker said that the firm gave the
the men to understand that they would rather
close their business than give the terms, notwith-
standing several other firms were honourably
keeping to their agreement, and he regretted that
Messrs. Corbett and M'Clymonts should be so
badly advised as to act as they had done. The
men, however, would manfully struggle, and
would not return to work unless they fulfilled the
conditions of the late settlement. A delegate con-
firmed the observutions of the former speaker. Mr.
Hearn advocated a like policy. These breaches of
faith he considered could not brook delay. The fol-
lowing resolution was then curried tmanimously :
" That this delegate meeting of house decorators
and painters earnestly urge the workmen lately
employed in the firm of Messrs. Corbett and
M'Clymonts to form a joint body to unitedly
tesist the attempted seduction of wages in that

firm, and this meeting pledges itself to support
the painters now on strike to the fullest extent in
our power."

TIIE LABOUItERS.—A large meeting of labourers
ployed in the building trade was held on Monday
night at the Lord Clyde, Pentonvillo-road, for the
purpose of promoting the interest of ale above

Mr. P. Konny,'lthe secretary of the Executive

length the circumstances attending the recent
dispute between the carpenters and masons and the
master builders, he remarked that the labourers,
owing to want of funds and proper organization,
were the principal sufferers from strikes and locks-

take country mansions, while the poor labourer,
after 25 years' hard work, had nothing left for
him but the workhouse. In any arbitration
on disputes between masters and men both sides
ohould be equally represented,

The chairman then read the following memorial
which had just been sent to the Master Builders'
Association:

Resolved—That, in the opinion of :the Builders'
Labourers' Union, numbering 2,500 members, the
halfpenny rise in our wages is not sufficient for us,
as provisions, clothing, and house rent have
risen to such an extent that our income cannot
meet our expenditure; we therefore solicit you to
give us the 6d. per hour, beginning on the Ist of
next March, 1873. If this memo:ial is not granted
by that date, we are prepared ,to take such steps
as we think are necessary to enforce it.—Edwin
Tough, President; P. Kenny, Executive Secre-
tary."

The Executive Council have also issued the
following appeal to the men:
"Fellow working men—lf the masters do not
concede the terms of our memorial, let us be pre-
pared to fight them for the 6d. per hour for
ordinary labourers, and the scalfolders to have the
same rate of wages as the mechanics; if not, let
them get men to erect the scaffolds for them, for
no union men will do it unless they get the wages.
So lot us strengthen our union, and by the let of
March, if the masters will receive another deputa-
tion, let us have man to man—not six to one
which is very unjust."
After some remarks from Mr. Halloran, who
stated that 250 men were being added to the
union weekly, a resolution was adopted establish-
ing an additional lodge, the members of which
are to meet at the Lord Clyde every Monday.
The union now consists of 15 lodges.

ANOTHER STRIKE. On Tuesday morning,
about 600 men of the building trade, includ-
ing carpenters, masons, bricklayers, plasterers,
painters, and labourers, struck work from the
firm of Messrs. Corbott and M'Clymont, the
builders and contractors at West Brompton, under
the following circumstances. Although the above
firm is unconnected with the Master Builders'
Association, at the request of their workmen they
began on Saturday, the 7th inst., to work under
the terms of the agreement entered into between
that association and the deputations from the
various trades, viz., 521 hours at Bid. per hour.
On Saturday last, however, upon the men going to
the pay-office for their money, they were paid at
the rate of 81d. per hour for the 521 hours they
had worked, but a printed notice was issued to
them that in future the wages would be only Sc!.
per hour. The men felt indignant at this breach
of faith on the part of their employers, and, instead
of resuming work on Monday morning, assembled
in general meeting, and appointed a deputation to
wait upon the firm. The deputation saw Mr
M'Clymont, who declined to withdraw the notice
Upon this decision being made known to the men,
they unanimously resolved to strike the firm until
the full terms of the agreement were conceded.
On Tuesday morning every man and boy on the
works, to the number of about 500, struck work,
and an executive committee of two delegates from
each branch of trade was appointed, who have
issued the following printed notice :
Caution.—To the Building Operatives of the
London District. —The firm of Messrs. Corbett
and M'Clyrnont, of Rodeliffe Estate, 13rompton,
having conceded and paid the new terms agreed to
by the Trades and the Master Builders' Associa-
tion, notice was given on Saturday, Sept. 14, that
a reduction of :Id. per hour would take place from
that date. Meetings of the various trades took
place this day, at which it was unanimously car-
ried that they should strike the firm until the full
terms of the late agreements are adopted, and we
ask you to refrain from seeking employment at the
firm until our dispute is settled.—By order of the
committee, Sept. 10.
The committee of the various trades to which
the operatives on strike belong have come forwar
with a promise to support the men, and a deputa-
tion from the carpenters who have struck (78 in
number) laid their ease before the carpenters' dele-
gate mooting, on Thursday evening, at the Brown
Bear, Bloomsbury, for the express purpose of deal-
ing with those firms who refuse compliance with
the terms of the new agreement.
Committee meetings of all the trades have been
held for the purpose of adopting measures to sup-
port the men on strike at Corbett and M'Cly-
mont's.

articles.title: SEPT. 21, 1872.
articles.text:
SEPT. 21, 1872.

AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS'

XOVEMEN T.

GREAT MEETING OF LABOURERS AT NEIVAIII.
On Tuesday night a largo meeting of labouring
men was held in the Newark Market-place to con-
sider the interests and prospects of the labour-
ing classes. The meeting, which was under the
auspices of the Newark Branch of the Lincolnshire
Agricultural Union, was originally intended to be
held in the Town Ilan, but as the authorities de-
termined to refuse that privilege, or right, the
promoters had no alternative but to resort to
nature's great public building—the Market-place.
At ten minutes past six a couple of waggons were
drawn up in front of the Town Ilall, around
which about 2,000 people assembled, and con-
ducted themselves in a very orderly manner indeed.
The speakers who then ascended the platform were
Professor Beesly, Mrs. Butler, Mr. George Potter,
Mr. B. Taylor, of Peterborough; Mr. Mitchell,
of London; Mr. Banks, of Boston; Mr. Boon,
Mr. Connoly, and others.
The chair was occupied by the Rev. S.
Robinson, the Unitarian minister of Newark, who
before opening the real meeting called upon Mr.
Banks, secretary of the Lincolnshire ,Association,
who read several letters and apologies from Mr.
P. A. Taylor., M.P., Mr. Trevelyan, ALP., Mr.
Mall, M.P., Mr. Jacob Bright, M. P and Pro-
fessor Stuart, expressing their sympathy with the
movement, and urging the labourers to seek their
ends by the exercise of political power.

The Chairman then offered a few remarks on
the subject of the meeting, stating that he was an
independent man, was not a member of the asso-
ciation, but had come before them because be
wished to cut down class interests, and gain for
the poor and helpless those rights which other
classes enjoy, believing that it would be to the ad-
vantage and welfare of the community.
Mr. Mitchell, of London, proposed the first
resolution as follows :

Taking into consideration the fact that the con-
dition of the agricultural and other unskilled
labourers of this country is a standing disgrace to
civilization and Christianity, and that other classes
of working men are making noble efforts to elevate
themselves, this meeting resolves that immediate
steps ought to be taken for the. improvement,
socially and politically, of the agricultural and
unskilled labourers of this country.
Mrs. Butler, who Feconded the motion, read a
speech, in which she said that her father was an agri-
culturalist named John Grey, of Northumberland.
He lived to the age of 83, and he spent his life in
seeking to improve the condition of the people. She
could not but think how deeply his heart would
have been stirred to assist in the great movement
which was now being inaugurated amongst the
labourers by representatives of their own class.
Her father always showed deep sympathy in such
objects as they were striving for, and it was oven
an axiom of his that in order to draw out all the
resources of agriculture, the culture of the mind
must precede that of the land, and he wished that
to apply to every individual alike, and wished to
see the blessing of education bestowed on the
honest labourers as well as upon the persons in the
higher walks of life.
The motion was then put and carried.

Mr. George Potter next addressed the meeting,
and concluded by moving the following:—
Taking into consideration the fact that combi-
nation has already done much to benefit skilled
labourers, this meeting is of opinion that the first
step, under the present system of competition,
towards the permanent improvement of agricul-
tural and other labourers is thorough combination,
and this meeting pledges itself to use every legal
means for the promotion of unionism. among the
agricultural and other unskilled labourers of this
country.
Mr. B. Taylor, of Peterborough, seconded the
motion in a most practical and energetic address,
pointing out that it was a delusion to say there
was no skill in ploughing straight and regular, in
shearing a sheep without clipping its skin, and in
packing a stack of bay in a proper manner ; and
stated also that the labourers were tho most nag"
lected about an estate, and the only remedy slis
unity of action and the exercise of political
power.
Mr. Connolly moved, and Mr. Boon seconded,
the following :
Seeing that the Game Laws are both unjust an,d
cruel, a prolific source of crime, and
especially heavy on all engaged in agriculture. 01'
meeting calls for the total repeal of the Gara°
Laws.
Smith
Professor Beesly moved, and Mr.
seconded :
That this meeting considers the Criminal LW°
Amendment Acta harsh, one-sided, and unnecessarYn_
law, and hereby pledges itself to use every mot 5
for its total repeal.
Mr. Banks moved, and Mr. Boon seconded t
That this meeting having learned with NKr°,
and consternation that soldiers hlive been allowr'
to interfere in disputes between employer and ern,
ployed, considers the same a dangerous precedeP

and most unconstitutional, and calls for a search-
ing and most impartial inquiry into the cause, and
pledges itself to use every legal means for the pre-
vention of such one-sided action by the War
Office officials in the future.
Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

articles.title: MEETING AT WISBEACII.
articles.text:
MEETING AT WISBEACII.

On Wednesday a largo demonstration of
labourers was held at Wisbeach, Cambridgeshire,
which was attended by the labourers and their
wives from the surrounding villages. The meet-
ing was preceded by a procession with band and
banners, and owing to the annual fair for the
hiring of servants being in Wisbeach, the pro-
ceedings attracted a great deal of attention.

B. Taylor, Esq., of Peterborough, occupied the
chair, and opened and conducted the proceedings
in a manner worthy of much commendation.

'Mr. Savage, a Cambridgeshire labourer, moved
the following resolution
That this meeting, deeply sympathizing with
the depressed condition of the agricultural
labourers of this county, pledges itself to use
every constitutional means to raise them to that
position in society which they are entitled to
occupy by obtaining a full compensation for their
labour.

Mr. Wills, of Wisbeach, seconded the motion,
and after Mr. George Potter had supported it in a
practical and vigorous speech, it was carried
unanimously.
Mr. G. Mitchell, of London, in a humorous
speech, in which he detailed his early life, moved
the following resolution :--
That this meeting believes that the woricing
men of this county can best elevate themselves by
forming associations, so that they can act in unity
with each other, and pledges itself to adopt that
course.

The resolution was seconded by Mr. :Trager-
dine, a tabourer of Wisbeach, and carried unani-
mously.
Mr. Balls, a labourer of Spalding, moved, and
Mr. Morris, a labourer of Peterborough, seconded,
the following resolution, which was carried by
acclamation :--

This meeting views with alarm the recent act of
the Government in sending soldiers into the
harvest field to supplant tho agricultural labourers,
and deprive them of their rights, there being no
Bearcity of hands, or refusal by any to do the
work, it also being well known that in some
counties the labourers' pay for harvest work did
not exceed 2s. 6d. per day; and that the Premier,
Mr. Gladstone, be asked to institute an inquiry
into the matter, for the purpoie of ascertaining
who is the person responsible for this act, and to
prevent the recurrence of such a step in the
future.

Tho proceedings closed with a hearty vof,, of
thanks to the chairman and speakers.

OPEN AIR MEETING AT POWERSTOCK.

On Wednesday evening last an open air meet-
ing of the Agricultural Labourers took place at
rowerstock, for the purpose of establishing a
Union in that district. The meeting commenced
at half-past 6 o'clock, under a wide-spreading elm
tree in the main thoroughfare of the village, and
there were between 200 and 300 people present.

Mr. Lockyor of Bridport, having been elected
chairman, opened the proceedings by remarking
that they had been sent there by the Agricultural
Union, for the purposenf giving them a short out-,
line of what the Union meant. It was composed
of a body of men, not for the purpose of creating a
disturbance, but for asking for that which men
simply called their rights. They knew that
agricultural men wore not wall paid for their
labour; no Ulan working twelve hours a day, and
only receiving 9E. a week, could _provide himself
with the necessaries of life, and bring up his
family properly at the same time. Ile had
been around Nettlecembe that evening, and ho
had been brought into contact with two or
three families of five and six children, and the
husband only getting 9s. per week. Sickness
prevailed in some of the families, and the dwellings
were or such a character that a respectable farmer
or landowner would not allow his dog to remain
in—rags were stuffed in the windows, and the rain
came through the roofs often while the poor in-
mates were in bed (" That's true " and " shame ").
What did the landlords care P Many of the men
worked till eight and ten at night and did not get a
penny extra. He would ask the question—what
did they get for it (A voice : Nothing). In the
face of all this endurance he urged upon them to
join the Union.

Mr. E. Snook, of• Blandford, the representative
of the National Union, then addressed the meet.
ing, and went on to speak of the immediate
advantages of the Union. They had a migration
company,
and by that means they had sent 15,000
men to America; if they were to join the Union
and were disposed to emigrate they could do so.
The 'Union would assist them in their every
endeavour to press for furthur increase of wages,
and he concluded by urging them to delay no time
in giving in theirs names and bixpenny subserip.
UM,

Several intimated their intention of doing so at
once, and there appeared to be every probability of
opening a branch in the district.
At a meeting of the London Trades Council on
Wednesday night, Mr. George Shipton, the
secretary, reported the receipt of the following
letter from the War Office, replying to one in
which complaint was made of the employment of
soldiers to get in the harvest in places where the
labourers were on strike :

Control Department, War Office,
Sept. 12, 1872.
Sir,—l am instructed by Mr. Secretary Cardwell
to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the
6th inst., and in reply to acquaint you that the
Queen's Regulations for the Army prescribe as
follows Art. 180. There will be no objection to
soldiers being allowed, at the discretion of general
officers in command, to assist in collecting the
harvest when application is made for that purpose,
provided that the employment of ,the population
is not thereby interfered with.' Mr. Cardwell has
directed inquiry to be made into the circumstances
under which soldiers were employed in the cases
to which you have referred, in order that he may
be informed whether any departure has occurred
in either instance from the letter or the spirit of
the regulation.—' am, Sir, your obedient servant,
T. VIVIAN.

After some discussion the council instructed the
secretary to write to Mr. Cardwell, strongly con-
demning the action taken by the War Office in
allowing the interference of soldiers in a dispute
between capital and labour. •

LABOUR MEETING AT PETRRBORI.

A meeting of laborers and other workmen took
place in the Labour Hall, Peterboro', on Friday
evening last, the building being well filled. The
objects, as stated, were to protest against the
recent employment of soldiers in the,harvest field;
to consider the workmen's trip to the sea side,
which was -postponed; to decide upon the pro-
gramme of action for the coming winter; as also
to consider the alleged threats held out by certain
employers; and to consider the opening of pro-
vision stores for the sale of bread, meat, flour, &a.
Mr. B. Taylor presided. The following resolution
was carried unanimously, amid much cheering
This meeting views with alarm the recent not
of the Government in sending soldiers into the
harvest field to supplant the agricultural labourers,
and deprive them of their rights, there being no
scarcity of hands, or refusal by any to do the
work, it also being well known that in some
counties the labourers' pay for harvest work did
not exceed 2s. 6d, per day; and that the Premier,
Mr. Gladstone, be asked to institute an inquiry
into the matter, for the purpose of ascertaining
who is the person responsible for this act, and to
prevent the recurrence of suoh a step in the
future.

The Chairman was requested to forward the
above resolution to the Prime Minister, and call
hi S attention thereto.

• The following letter and petition have been pre

To A. M. Cunynghame, Esq., secretary, General

Edinburgh, Sept; 12, 1872.
TloNeunp Srn,—We, the letter-carriers of
Edinburgh and Leith, respectfully bog to present

TEE INTERNATIONAL IN LONDON.

At a very large meeting of the British Federal
Council of the International, held at the offices, 7,
Hed Lion-court, Fleet•street, on Thursday even-
ing last, the following resolution was proposed by
Citizen Hales, late general seeretary of the
St. Luke's branch, and carried by a very largo
majority :—" Resolved, that this council thorofighly
iepudiates the imputation made by Dr. Marx at the
Congress of The Hague, when, in advocating the
admission to the congress of Maltman Barry as
delegate of a Gorman section in Chioago after his
expulsion from the British Federal Council, he
said 'that it was rather an honour than otherwise
not to be a leader of the English working class, as
the majority of those leaders were sold.' " An
addendum also moved by Citizen Hales, declaring
it to be the opinion of the council "That Dr. Marx
did not believe the charge himself, but made it to
serve a personal purpose," was lost by the casting
vote of the chairman. Citizen Hales then gave
notice of motion that Dr. Marx was no longer fit
to be a member of the association. Citizen G. B.
Clarke gave notice that he should propose that the
council 'should repudiate the acts of the Hague
Congress on the ground that they, were illegal and
subversive of the principles of the association.

The Federal Council of the International and
adhering society opened a Congress on Monday
evening at the New Hall of Science, Old-street,le
which the general public wore admitted on pay-
merit, but the 'attendance was very limited, there
not being more than about a hundred persons pre-
sent; amongst them, however, were several fe-
males. The proceedings were carried on in
English, French, German, and Polish—a president
for each section being chosen—Wesley, liandeck,
Schreider, and Militsky.
The presidents having examined and verified the
mandates of the delegates, it was announced that
there were representatives of English, French,
German, and Polish societies jpresent at the Con-
gress. '

Citizen Landeck then rose to open the discus-
sion, and spke on the influence exercised by the
International on the Empire, the Government of
the National Defence, and of the Commune, and
on the enfranchisement of the working classes.
lie complained of the conduct of the Commune
for their moderation, and said there was now set
up in London an aristocracy which for two months
had mismanaged Paris when everything was in
their own hands, They were now the followers
of Marx who had sown such discord in the Inter-
national. Ile declared there was a total absence
of revolutionary ideas in the society, the objects of
which were that men should be properly rewarded
for their toil, and those only
.who worked should
receive reward.

Citizen Smith followed with espeeeb, in which
he disclaimed all revolutionary,spirit on the part
of the International.

Citizen Lundy then moved the following resolu-
tion :---

Considering that the International Association
of Working Men has for its object the emancipa-
tion of workmen oy thomselves--bonsidering that
the General Council of the International nomi-
nated to carry out this programme has, on thtk
contraty, affirmed an authoritative principle —a
principle contrsry to the principles of the Inter-
national and to the interests of the working-classes
—this Congress blames the conduct of
,the Inter-
nationa,l in its past, and proposes a revision of the
statutes and of the rules on the basis of Com-
munalist and Federelist principles.

This resolution was seconded by M. Zielienski,
and supported by Mr. Green.
Citizen Funnell moved an amendment; to the
effect that the consideration of the question should
be postponed.

Several citizens addressed the meeting in French
and German, and after aAomewhat exalted debate
a division was taken, when the members were—
Fur the amendment, 10; against it, 17. The
original motion was accordingly carried.
The sitting was then adjourned to Tuesday
evening, a vote of thanks to the Chairman
,having
been passed.
On Tuesday the proceedings were opened by a
speech from Citizen Schneider, in which he insisted
on the necessity of watching over the policy of the
International, for it was the power destined to
liberate the working classes. What is to be done,
ho asked, to liberate ourselves? Empires, royalty,
and finance are international, wily should not the
working classes be international also? In order
to become international we must permit great
local independence to the nations where the laws
against the International are stringent. They
should not be called upon to compromise them-
selves by subscriptions. Citizen Smith, who had
been acting as translator, delivered a speech in
English and in French, in which he urged the
democrats to join every movement, however mode-

would gain renown, andimight ultimitely lead the

They should act like the Scotchman who took all

recently, been observed respecting the groivth of
corals. Somewhat less than two years ago Captain
liGregor, of the steamer Kilauea, moored a buoy
in Kealakokua Bay. Last week he was ordered
to hoist the anchor and examine the condition of
the chain. The latter, which is a heavy two-inch
cable, N% as found covered with corals and oyster

submerged. The specimen which we have seen

protection. The popular supposition is that corals
are of extremely slow growth. Here we have a
formation equal to over 17ft. in a century.—
Honolulu Gazette.

SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 21, 1872.

THE INTERNATIONAL.

THERE are many points connected with the
policies of the various governments of Europe
upon which those who live by their labour
should seek to understand each other. Work.
ing men, all the world over, have common
interests, and. should therefore, wherever
possible, have common thoughts in reference
to these interests. How to get together
that they may endeavour to understand each
other, or how to establish an accepted organ
for the purpose of exchanging and comparing
ideas, are questions of serious moment. There
can be no use in bringing Frenohmen,
Spaniards, Italians, Germans, Danes, Swedes,
Americans, and Englishmen together merely
to express their common and deelpy-folt
hatreds of those who oppress and injure them.
Reason, not passion, should be the bond by
which they are united, and practical prima
-
pies applicable to every-day life should supplY
the staple of discussion when their represen•
tatives meet.

If the men who belong to the International
Society represented all ranks and classes, their
discussions should include questions of general
national policy connected with the well-being
of nations. That they were not men of
this kind we may take for granted, inasmuch
as the list of delegates present at the
Hague did not contain even one solitary name
known as belonging to any great thinker.
Possibly there were men of intelligence
and activity at the Congress willing
to do what good they could, but there
does not seem to have been anybody present
who could be fairly taken as representing any
great principle or living thought, or who, in
any way on the road of progress, is recognized
as an advanced or influential leader.
If, on the other hand, the International
Society does not represent the nations gene-
rally, if their object be to specially promote the
interests of the working classes, their discus-
sions should have been chiefly confined to the
elucidation and enforcement of ideas connected
with working men's interests, and above all
things, they should have included in their
numbers men recognized as leaders amongst
working men, thus guaranteeing a living
power behind them, that would count for
something in the great fight of principles, by
which sensible men hope to win the freedeat
of the world, In this respect the list of
names was as barren as in the case alreadY
mentioned. We looked in vain for the name
of any English delegate, who could be said ill
any proptr sense to represent any phew 0,
English thought, or any known body °I
English working men. As leaders of men, or
propagators of thought, they are Bin'PlY
nobodies, without influence of any kind what-

ever. We do not say that the name of any
one of them was never heard before ; we
simply wish to be understood as asserting that
those present would not be accepted by any
large body of men in England as their
exponents or representatives. They did not
represent any of our great trades organiza-
tions, nor, in fact, bodies of Englishmen of
any sort, organized for the promotion of a
thought or an interest of any kind connected
with the industrial masses of our people.
In what sense then, we ask, eau Such a
gathering be called " International ?" No
great thought, no leading popular idea, no
great movement in connection with any
popular demand. Every well-wisher of our
working people would have rejoiced if the
gathering at the Hague gave proof that the
men assembled were able to grapple with
living questions. They did not attempt such
a thing, and, therefore, instead of useful work
we have only practical evils conspicuously con-
nected with their proceedings.

In the first place, for reasons already given,
this assemblage, in any national or interna-
tional sense, was a sham. In the next place,
according to the most favourable reports fur-
nished to the public, all the delegates left
behind them local quarrels, and as soon as
they met entered on a general row, which
continued as long as the assembly held to-
gether. This we are painfully conscious of,
but we are not conscious that they pledged,
or had any power to pledge, the people of
their various nations to united action on un-
derstood progressive principles. We are also
painfully conscious that they did not trust
each other as honest politicians, suspicions of
espionage and treason evidently troubling the
minds of a considerable number. Why such
suspicions should exist in an assembly of
which English working man formed a part, it
is hard to say; but where there is felt a
necessity for closed doors and secret delibera-
tions, despots, of whatever colour, will
naturally enough make provision for dis-
covering what takes place, and in this case it
is fair to conclude that there was very solid
ground for the irritating distrust so strongly
expressed.

One of the worst features of such a
gathering, however, is to be found in the
means of injury it places in the hands of those
opposed to popular progress. An assembly
which quarrels when it ought to be in calm
deliberation, ardent patriots bent on the
liberation of the world discussing whether
their subscriptions should be a penny a month
or a penny a year, do not furnish a sight free
from excitements to banter even to those who
are anxious to see good liberal work going
forward. But the newspaper press and the
rulers in whose interests it is active and
zealous, do not hold up to ridicule such
weakness. Their policy is of a different kind.
They exaggerate the power and importance of
such an association, because they desire to
increase the fears and alarms of the timid and
feeble in relation to it. Despots cannot but
be delighted with proceedings which travestie
liberal principle and sound honest thought,
and which discredit sensible practical move-
ments in favour of human freedom in thought
and action. They find in these assemblages a
means of justification for anything they may
do to impede the liberating march of modern
thought. Nobody—not even CARL MARX
himself—knows better than the three Em-
perors recently met in conclave, how divided,
feeble, and purposeless the International is.
How little real hold it has on working men
throughout Europe, especially in Great
Britain, where liberty of speech smothers in
its own offensiveness extravagance of thought.
In the interest of Liberal progress the re-
moval of the head-quarters of this association
to New York is a matter to rejoice at, as its
eccentricities there will neither be so singular
nor so mischievous as in Europe. The free
people and free Government of the great Re-
public render extravagances of thought harm.
less by permitting men to get weary of their
own ludicrous follies. They are subjects of
pity or amusement there; here they are dis-
crediting and injurious. Our working men
need for the improvement of their social and
political condition, serious, honest, open work;
nothing (450 can profit them. rrepostorous

shams, serving only the sinister purposes of
despots, are things to be avoided. We have
neither time nor inclination to play at hide
and seek with reactionary Governments. Our
labours as a people on behalf of political and
social progress must be honest, open, and
above-board. Our highest advantages will
be found in the peaceable improvement of the
laws and usages of society, and we can best
succeed in this by taking the whole world into
our confidence, and thus finding auxiliaries
everywhere amongst the friends of even-
handed justice and rational liberty.
In urging this view of the ease we do not
wish to have our Internationals deprived in
any way oflitheir rights of extravagance; we
simply desire to have it understood, as an
absolute truth, that whatever their influence
or power may amount to elsewhere, in Eng-
land, either individually or together as a
society, they are powerless, a bugbear to
others and a trouble to themselves. Since
the English delegates have returned home
they have as good as repudiated CARL
MARX, and set up an International concern of
their own. We do not feel any inclination to
meddle between such parties; we simply con-
sider it a pity that the action of the Liberal
party in England should be encumbered by
men incapable of appreciating true inter-
national ideas, or of conducting themselves
towards each other in a manner creditable to
the principles they profess to admire and
uphold.

THE BAKERS' STRIKE SUPERSEDED.
WE have to congratulate the master and
journeyman bakers of London upon the amicable
and mutually satisfactory terms on which
they have settled the questions on which they
were at issue. A section of the masters were
contemplating a different result. In the cal-
culation that the men would be driven to put
in force their threat, a leading firm largely
circulated an address to mistresses of house-
holds, offering them "flour, yeast, &e., with
printed instructions for making bread," and,
of course, enclosing the masters' version of
the matters in dispute. As another master
candidly confessed, however, the men had the
best of it, both as to the merits and as to the
superior manner in which they had known
how to conduct their proceedings. Judging
by results, this compliment was not un-
deserved; for, with one exception, the men
have gained, without a strike, and by fair and
open argument, all the points for which they
contended.
At tho last hour, as might have been ex-
pected, the high and mighty section of the
masters made one more effort to provoke a
no-surrender issue. The masters had not con-
oeded the four-to-four principle. If the men so
understood, they made a great mistake. How,
asked the mover of the masters' amendment,
could a motion be considered as binding on
both parties, when the men only, and not the
masters, voted upon it. The obvious reply is,
that the masters had the opportunity, and
have themselves to blame that they did not
use it. In fact, as the chairman felt con-
strained to rule, the four-to-four principle,
pure and simple, had been adopted,
" though," so far as the masters were con-
cerned, "in a negative sense; " which is to
say, we suppose, that they could not help
themselves.

The men have won this, to them, great
victory by a judicious conjunction of firm-
ness and moderation. They resolved not to
flinch under any circumstances from their
main point—a working day of twelve hours,
counting from four after midnight to four
after noon; and the demand was, by all
impartial persons, and even by many of their
own employers, felt to be so reasonable, that
inflexible insistency on this point was the
surest road to success. The men had the
good fortune to be led by individuals of their
own class, who commanded and deserved their
confidence. When the question was put,
were all satisfied with the delegates appointed
to represent them in a conference with the
representatives of the employers, every hand
was held up in the affirmative. They thus
had the advantage of perfect union. When,
too, it was asked whether they would abide
by whatever result might come out of the

meeting between the delegates of the two
parties, there was a similar manifestation of
unanimous acquiescence. This gave to those
in viliose bands they were entrusting their
cause the strengthening and animating feel-
ing that they were not going to labour in vain,
or to spend their strength for nought.
At the: third conference between the master
and men delegates, when the subordinate
" sponge " question had been disposed of, it
quickly appeared that the qualification with
which the masters were willing to concede the
four-to-four principle, would never go down
with the men. —With a seriousness and
sobriety of tone that must have been vcry
striking to thoughtful minds among the masters,
they were answered that the subjected had been
looked at on the part of the:men as completely as
was possible from the masters' own point of view;
and yet, out of the three-and-forty branches
into which the trade had been divided for
organization and deliberation, only two more
than the odd threelwere in the least degree
willing to yield to the neutralising condition
with which the masters wanted to cripple and
spoil the clear and moderate principle con-
tended for.

At the fourth and final conference the
attendance was full on both sides. Overtime was
the only matter which remained over for par-
ticular discussion, the scale of wages having
been previously disposed of in a manner
mutually satisfactory. Now, it was not
attempted, on either hand, to conceal the fact
of a diversity of businesses as requiring
different modes of dealing with them. In
reference to this, and indeed to the whole
question, Mr. WESTON, the chairman, took
notice of the suggestion which we had thrown
out, as one adapted to prove to masters and
men that they had a common interest in the
maintenance of the London trade as it now
stands. If,..he said, through any action taken
by masters and men the production of bread
was affected, there would be a great temptation
for capitalists to embark in the trade; and by
the introduction of machinery, the labour
would be to a great extent superseded. He
would beg to inform them, that he had a
maehine with which, under certain conditions,
he could mix and make into dough from six-
teen to eighteen sacks of flour an hour. Mr.
WEsTox, however, no doubt sees that there is
no reason whatever in the nature of things,
why the bread required for the consumption of
more than three millions of mouths in and
around London, should not be made and baked
many miles beyond the metropolitan radius.
Happily for both parties, they have, for the
present at least, averted this danger, rather,
perhaps, this disturbance.
The question of Sunday baking, though
secondary to that of the length of the working
hours on the other six days of the week, has
formed an interesting feature in these trade
discussions. The point was introduced by a
journeyman, whose employer, though serving
a crowded locality, had been able to get rid of
this burden for the last nine years. In fact,
the desire to shut up bakers' ovens on the day
of rest has been expressed in various forms
for upwards of half a century, though hitherto
it has been deemed sufficient to answer that,
looking at the matter from the point of view
of either mere rest or positive religion, mere
rest and air, at liberty to go to church, or to
chapel, by people's dinners being baked at the
bakehouse than if they were cooked at home.
This, however, is a view which could not be
expected to be accepted with contentment by
the men who lost their Sunday in order that

everybody besides might have it for rest or
play, or any purpose that pleased them.
"Why," as Mr. BAINES demanded, "should
they, any more than other mechanics, be com-
pelled to work on Sundays?" As between
masters and. men it came to this : whether, as
the men proposed, Sunday bakings should be
"abolished," or, as the masters would have
had it, that they are, indeed, "a wrong done
to the journeymen," and that, therefore,
they (the masters) will use their moral
influence to bring about their abolition.
It did not appear that the mode in
which the masters would fain have nulli-
fied. the four-to-four principle, had prepared
the men to rely very trustfully upon the use
of their moral illatloUO4 ill any mattor 111

portant to their working hands. Nevertheless,
the men were too well aware of the rootedness
of old customs to be stubborn in a case of
subordinate, though not unimportant, moment
to themselves; in a case, too, where it could
hardly be supposed that their employers had,
much at stake to make them less desirous of
a free Sabbath than their assistants. The
whole meeting, therefore, was content that it
should be as one master, on behalf of the
whole, proposed, not total and immediate
abolition, but abolition Lby means of moral
influence; and, upon the whole, the general
feeling between the parties?, appeared to be
promising.

The best feeling between masters and men
came out on both sides during the discussions
as to overtime. A general resolution, pro:.
posed by a journeyman, to the effect that,
where the plant is so, large as to make night
work unavoidable, night men may be employed
from mid- night to eight in the morning, met
with support from both men and masters; but,
in the end, it was ordered to lie on the table,
on the ground that, though carried, it would
be of non-effect till agreed to unanimously by
both masters and men. The price for overtime
per hour was most satisfactorily and amicably
arranged. A certain scale having been
moved by one journeyman, a second rose, and,
observing that, as a body of working men,
they would like to see a little concession
made, proposed a somewhat lower scale, to
which a leading master assented, with the
difference that foremen only should have nine-
pence instead of a shilling as first proposed,
and that second and third hands should have
sixpence alike, instead of sixpence to the
former and but fourpence to the latter; and,
in this amended form, the scale was unani-
mously adopted.

articles.title: ALEXANDRA. PARK.
articles.text:
THE ALEXANDRA. PARK.

IF the promoters of the Alexandra Park scheme
mean that it should turn out a success they
should press it forward without unnecessary
delay. It would be waste of time to urge the
necessity of such an undertaking in the interest
of the working people of the country. Tho
cry heard on all sides is for more leisure for
our working people, and in all recent move-
ments on the part of those engaged in active
bodily employment, the demand is that a
larger proportion of the twenty-four hours
should be devoted to rest and recreation than
has hitherto been employed in that way.
Naturally enough, following this comes the
query how this time is to be spout? We are
not amongst those who believe that as a rule
it will be mis-spent. We do not demand
higher virtues from the working class than
from any other class
.of the community; but
we are quite satisfied that when the hours of
labour are shortened, opportunities of seeking
improvement:of mind and health of body should
be furnished, or the good counted on will not be
realised to its full extent. Large as the pro
vision by parks is in London and its immediate
neighbourhood, much is yet wanted for the
accommodation of its vast population. Where-
ever access can be obtained to the green sward,
overcrowding is the rule—there the people
flock to enjoy the coolness and freshness of the
summer air.

No more needed or appropriate blessing could,
therefore, be offered to working men than a
park with provisions adapted to their require-
ments. We are quite sure that if the LORD
litAyou and the gentlemen associated with him
can secure the Alexandra Park at a reasonable
price, the working classes will help effectuaully
in carrying out so excellent a project. And as
such a property might he made to suit the
wants of people in the provinces as well as
those belonging to the metropolis, there is no
reason why so laudable a scheme should net
be taken up with something approaching a
national enthusiasm.

It has been. rumoured that those who have
at present got:it in their hands are trying to
exact unwarrantable conditions. If this be so,
though it is to be regretted, it is no reason
why so good a project should be given up.
There are no doubt other places which might
be obtained for the sum which, under the
most favourable conditions of sale, will have
to he paid for Alexandra Park, and the mar!
mittee might yely reasonably t,akQ telm wittl

the view of ascertaining whether such be the
ease. Such a property as this Park cannot be
much sought after as a single purchase, and
the proprietors, or those who act for them,
would do well, we think, not to oppose need-
less difficulties between themselves and those
who are willing to become purchasers for an
object so excellent as that contemplated by
the LORD Mnron and the committee acting
with him. It is quite time, at any rate, that
some kind of information should be given by
the committee to the public on a subject so
interesting.

articles.title: BALLOT AT PRESTON.
articles.text:
THE BALLOT AT PRESTON.

Tun Conservatives have been boasting of
their victory at Preston under the Ballot, and
they have a perfect right to do so. We never
for a moment imagined the Ballot would in
any way change the current of political
thought, or alter the complexion of party pre-
judice. In tho big towns there has not been
for a long time much chance of putting on the
screw to obtain votes. The artizan, whether
in defence of his convictions or his stupidities,
is, as a rule, a sturdy man, not to:be easily
driven from any ground he may take up. The
gain from the Ballot in our big towns will be
a gain in the interests of sobriety and order,
not a slight gain, as we know by our election
experience; and in addition to this a very im-
portant benefit in freedom from bribery nearly
always practised when electioneering contests
are doubtful as to result. On these points
there is every reason to believe that the Ballot
will be perfectly successful, and this is cer-
tainly no slight praise to bestow on it.
As to the Conservative victory few will
either be surprised or disappointed by it. The
Conservatives are loud in their expressions of
triumph, but, so far as they are concerned as a
" national " party, wo cannqt see what they
have gained. We say as a national party,
seeking to benefit the country by the introduc-
tion of better principles into national law, and
a sounder policy into the practices of our
national Government. What is Mr. HOLKER
distinguished for? Wherein does he differ
from Major GERMAN in regard to
.such matters?
if the Standard, the Globe, or any other Con-
servative organ could point to distinguishing
principles, or higher policies in the thought of
110LKEn over GERMAN, it would, we are sure,
be a great comfort to their readers. Neither
of these respectable prints will, we are sure,
attempt suoh a thing, as they know quite as
well as we do, that they would be sure to fail
in such an effort. They have, it is quite true,
gained, rather than lost, a vote in the House.
They have prevented their approach to office
being made more difficult, and this is some-
thing, so far as their leaders and their tag-rag
of office expectants are concerned, but we do
not see that the nation can gain anything by
the mere accession to office of Mr. DISRAELT
and his friends.

If, however, the Liberals care anything
about the matter, this defeat carries with it
an excellent lesson. The party called
Liberal is becoming afraid of its own prin-
ciples, and its candidates are chosen because
they stand. near the Conservatives rather than
because they stand well out in advance of
them. The constituencies arc puzzled mote
by resemblance than difference in those who
solicit their suffrages. They can hardly make
up their minds whether to prefer Comm' to
SHOUT or SUM' to CODLIN, and this confusion
of ideas will continue till Conservative and
Liberal policies become as separate and dis-
tinct as in the old days, when compromises and
compliances were not as fashionable as they
are at the present moment.

It may be a pity Major GETMAN did not go
in for Preston; if so it is because it threatens
Mr; GLADSTONE'S position, notbecause the nation
is in any way likely to suffer from such an event.
We believe the Ballot will be very much more
felt in - the counties than in the ities and
boroughs, and we are quite sure it will lead to
a new set of questions amongst our rural
population. If, however, things remain pretty
much as they are, undisturbed by the introduc-
tion of new questions, or the appearance of new
men with clearer ami more earnest convictions,
we have nothing for it as Liberals but to
bear with what we have brought into
xistenee by our own labours. Advanced

Liberalism may be a very good thing, but if
the country does not want it, to try to force it
would be a folly, The Whigs have had a
tolerably long inning, and, as we all know,
"turn about is fair play." The working men
have, no doubt, something to say whenever
they make up their minds to speak out. At
present they are satisfied to run at the heels of
others, and to shout as they are ordered. A
commercial panic, which prophets of evil are
already beginning to foresee, may shake things
out of their old groves and give the necessary
audacity for the utterance of something
stronger as political thought than we have had
an opportunity of listening to lately. Out of
evil comes good, at least our political ex-
perience as a nation countenances the belief
that our politicians are disinclined to move
unless urged forward by the goad of necessity.
Of the Preston election it may be said that
it would be impossible to conceive a more
bare-faced attempt to defeat the object of law
than that of the Conservative agents as de-
scribed by their friends in the. Conservative
papers. The object of the Conservatives in
the House of Commons, as well as that of a
considerable number of sham Liberals, was
how to make an act which could be broken
through, and it must be confesed that they
succeeded. By their past practices they have
called into life unprincipled agents of all
calibres in rascality, fellows who could rifle
the coffers of a bank, or strip a henroost.
Whether honest men will stand quietly by and
allow such a corrupt and, corrupting scum to
Wrest the law to their evil purposes remains
to be Seen. If the decent men decide other-
wise their action should be quick and decisive.
The rogues have described their own game,
and if a general election be permitted to take
place without some alteration in the law
which shall prevent its repetition, it will be
a disgrace alike to the Legislature and the
country.

articles.title: IMPERIAL CONSPIRACY.
articles.text:
THE IMPERIAL CONSPIRACY.

A VIENNA paper (the raterland) publishes
an outline of the scheme concocted at the
recent meeting by the three Emperors. In
the first place, they reciprocally guarantee
each other—a very natural undertaking if
they can carry it out, but it would be very diffi-
cult to find in such guarantee anything very
consolatory as regards the peace and freedom
of Europe. Such a compact, however, may
be regarded chiefly as a hint to France of the
danger lurking ,behind any attempt to alter
her present restricted boundaries. The second
point refers to the business and intercourse of
the subjects of the three Empires and the
third provides for the removal by Russia of coin-
mereial restrictions, and contains permission to
Russia, as a compensation, to increase her
navy in the Black Sea. But the most im-
portant of all, and that which will be most
heartily prosecuted and vigilantly carried out,
is a: mutual pledge to consolidate the monar-
chical principle in Europe, by a rigorous
supervision of the press and, a repression of
democratic and aocialiskogitations.
Who can doubt the sincerity of spirit in
whioh this last engagement was made. A war
against such agitations simply means a war
against free thought. Not because democracy
and. socialism may be considered the truest
forms of thought, but because despots in the
very nature of things late free discussion, and
under these names a crasade against all
thought dangerous to their power will be
mercilessly and unrelentingly carried on.
Other points of agreement are spoken of,
especially one as to the attitude of the three
Powers in relation to the Roman Catholic
Church. This, however, is a secondary consider-
ation. Catholic claims are well-known and un-
derstood. The adherents of the Porn possess no
novelty of thought nor any hidden unmea-
sured force. Whatever it may amount to, it is
a declining not a growing power. What it
can do, when all its agencies are set in
motion, as well as what it cannot do, are
matters with which the statesmen of Europe ,
have -become acquainted by a long study.
But the new thought, the modern force,which
is penetrating and operating everywhere
disquiets them. What they denominate
democracy and. socialism are subtle influences
Bpreading daily, penetrating their dominions

at all points, and against these they will fight
with all the skill and power they possess.
What truth generally there may be in the
statements of the Vetterland, we cannot pre-
tend to say, but that this one important portion
of the Imperial conspiracy rests on fact, we
have no doubt whatever.

articles.title: SPANISH PROSPECTS.
articles.text:
SPANISH PROSPECTS.

TuE King of SPAIN has opened the Cortes.
His reference to the PorE, who likes neither
him nor his father, was judiciously temperate.
Like the King of ITALY, he respects, and even
"venerates," the spiritual power; yet he is
firmly resolved to maintain the laws made "by
the will of the Spanish nation." Thus, if the
people will stand by him, he will stand by
them ; if not, like the first King of the
BELGIANS, he says, let me know that you do
not want me, and I will leave you. The
speeches of his Minister ZORILLA are in the
same key and tone. Ho will govern, not for
party, but for the community; and he will
defend the dynasty of his Constitutional
King, if necessary with his blood. Three-
fourths of the people's representatives are
with him, not including the out-and-out
Republicans, who, if he act as he speaks, will
be drawn after him., In the Senate he can
reckon upon an equal amount of support.
What is best is, that the elections which have
yielded these results, were perfectly free and
unconstrained. His worst enemies and the
KING'S are those very men who thought to
make AMADEUS their tool, and he will be no
man's tool. Ho tried them all by turns, and
none of them was able to hold his ground.
ZORILLA had retired in digust to his country
seat when the KING called for his services.
Let it be hoped that the Spaniards will know
their day of salvation. •

articles.title: PRIESTS AND THE GOVERNMENTS.
articles.text:
THE PRIESTS AND THE GOVERN-
MENTS.

THE war proceeds between the high sacer-
dotal party and the civil Governments of
Germany and Italy. The refractory BISHOP of
ERMELAND would, perhaps, have the best of it
were the EMPEROR his solo adversary in cor-
respondence. His IMPERIAL MAJESTY simply
tells the haughty prelate that all he wants
from him is a statement of his willingness to
obey the laws. The Churchman answers by
acknowledging an "unlimited sovereignty"
in civil matters, but in matters of faith he
can only bow to the Church. When it comes,
to Prince 13isituncies turn he calls for a dis-
tinct admission from the Bintor that in ex-
communicating without previous intimation
of his intention to the Government he dis-
obeyed the law of the laud. Priestlike, the
wily Prelate pretended a discrepancy between
the EMPEROR'S letter and his Minister's, with
more to the same purport. To this the CIEAN•-
CELLOR conclusively replies that his Right
Reverend correspondent has not improved.
matters, but has rather made them worso,.
and, at all events, has given no answer to his
plain call for a confession that he broke the
laws.

Some people are weak enough to believe that
priests are an improved sort of' persons. But,
while in one of the German provinces we
have this unmanageable Bishop wriggling
instead of being straightforward, we have,
in the new province of Alsace, a good
story to prove that the priests of 1872 rely
upon the same tricks as their predecessors
before the Reformation. The Jesuits, highly
resenting their expulsion, wish to persuade
the peasantry that the wrath of Heaven is
excited. in their favour. In a village near
Strasburg, the VIRGIN MART appeared,
for the
purpose of exhorting them to take up arms for
the priests. The German commandant sent
a detachment of dragoons to the village,
where, as usual, the " Mother of God" made
herself visible. The sentry challenged in
military form, but,she made no answer. After
three " sommations," without more success,
he fired. The wounded VIRGIN turned out to
be" a. very fat cure," whose lusty cries made
the night hideous. He is having his wound
dressed in the hospital, and three other
priests, suspected of having dressed him in
the character, of the Blessed Virgin, are in
custody.

The POPE, himself, is so much excited that
his phlegmatic Councillor, ANTONIELLI, cannot

SEPT.: 21,187

restrain him. He seizes every occasion
.f,t?
fulminating diatribes against ~ Emperor,,
Kings, Ministers, Parliaments, and people,
until he makes himself black in the face, sn4.
coughs as if he would burst a blood• Vessel.
The Jesuit Fathers in the Holy City are e 09,1!
enough, having not lost a jot of that modest
assurance which was always one of the chief,
attributes of their order. The xnuniciPal
authorities of the Italian capital resolved. to .
mark with inscriptions the.places of historic 4 I
interest. In what is now the French Academy
at Rome, the great astronomer GAILEO
was tortured by the Inquisition for affirming,,
that the earth revolves round the sun. The
FRENCH AMBASSADOR to the Court of Italy, ;
waited on the Mayor of ROME imploring him net.

articles.title: LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.
articles.text:
LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

The first meeting of the London School
Board after the vacation was held on Wed-
nesday at Guildhall; Lord Lawrence in the
chair.

On the motion of Mr. Lucraft, permission
was given to the managers of the Windsor-
street Board School to establish an evening
school in accordance with the resolution of the
Board of July 12, 1871, and the New Code of
Regulations, 1872.
The following alteration in the scale of
teachers' salaries was adopted on the motion of
Mr. McGregor :
A payment will be made, for holding an evening
school, of 15s. for every scholar up to 25 inclusive,
and of 10s. for every scholar beyond that number
who attends 60 times during the year and passes
the Government examination. In addition, the
teacher will receive £5 a quarter for the two
quarters during which the school will be opened.
Alliarrangements as to the number of weeks in the
year, and of nights in the week, for which the
school is to be held, and as to the fees, &e., must
first be submitted for the approval of the Board.
The report of the Works' Committee was
received, on the proposition of Mr. C. Reed,
M.P., the vice-chairman.
On the motion of the hon. member, the seal
of the Board was affixed to an appointment of
Mr. Edward Ryde as arbitrator on behalf of
the Board in the matter of the purohase of the
interest of Mr. Thomas Jones in certain
premises situate in St. John's-lane Clerken-
well, in respect of which the Board have
served a notice to treat. _ _

The business, which lasted less than half
an hour, was routine, and an adjournment for
a week was taken.
