articles.title: LORD CARNARVON ON WORKING
articles.text:
LORD CARNARVON ON WORKING

MEN'S CLUBS.

On Monday afternoon Lord Carnarvon laid
the foundation stone of a Working*Men's Club,
at Carlton, near Nottingham. • The building is
to be erected entirely at the cost of the Hon.
and Rev. 0. W. Forester, vicar, of the parish.
Lord Carnarvon, addressing the working men
present, said that if there was one institution in
England more particularly English than another
he thought it was the institution of clubs. Now,
they very often read about the London .clubs, and
he would tell them what those clubs were. The
London club was a large house, very comfortably
fitted up, to which a number of gentlemen sub-
scribed every year a moderate awn of money,
where they could dine, interchange opinions
frankly and freely, and where they could meet
their own friends and acquaintances—where, in
short, they enjoyed all the advantages of a large
house and establishment for a very small expen-
diture. And just as this had been so very
popular with the one class, he never could see why
it should not be adopted by other classes in the
country. He understood that in the club, the found-
ation-stone of which he had just laid, they would
have all the principal elements and characteristics
which the London clubs possessed. They would
have food for the mind and food for the body. lie
hoped before very long there would be a very good
library formed within its walls' as books were now
very cheap—good ones as well as indifferent ones.
He hoped there would also be the leading
periodicals and newspapers; for in nothing had
there been a greater improvement than in tho
periodical literature of the time. It had become
higher, better, and purer within his memory than
any other branch he know; and he would suggest
to those who would have a share in the manage-
ment of the club that they should take in literature
which represented fairly the different political
opinions of the day, but have none of the vile and
scurrilous literature which sometimes disgraced the
age in which we lived. There would be refresh-
ment, also, for the body; not only tea and coffee
and those beverages which cheered but did not
inebriate, but also—and he thought it was decided
very wisely—there would be facilities to have
good, wholesome English beer, He was a great
advocate for good English beer, and thought there
was nothing better and more truly English
altogether. Now, he had ventured to put in a
plea for another °hiss of refreshment; he had
said to Mr. Forester that he hoped tobacco would
not be excluded, and Mr. Forester at once adopted
the plea. There were very many excellent persons
who found fault with smoking, and said it was a
terrible vice, and led to drinking with all other
abominations. Now, he was not one of those; he
believed, on the contrary, as Shakespeare said of
wine, that "it was a good creature if it was well
used ;" and so he (his lordship) thought of the
tobacco-pipe. They were told it was slow poison.
Well, he answered, that it must be a very
slow poison indeed, because seine of his oldest
and best friends had smoked all their lives,
and wore as well and hearty as they were
twenty-years ago. The doctors told us that
while tobacco was more extensively used than
over before, there was a steady., marked increase
in tho average length of life. He rejoiced, there-
fore, that those who wished might use tobacco in
that club. A billiard table would also be provided.
There might be some persons who were afraid.
His answer was, it had been tried in London and
had not been abused; awl he had sufficient cod,-
dence in his fellow-countrymen to feel that when
these things were placed within their reach they
would use them as sensible men' as they did other
good gifts which it had pleased God to give uti to
increase our happiness, remembering that they
were not the things on which our time and energy
should be absorbed. After observing that it was
the intention of lAdy. Carnarvon and himself to
add a bowling green to the amusements of the
club as a mark of their goodwill and sympathy
with the work, his lordship said the success or the
failure of the club depended upon the working
men who had the management of it, and upon
them alone. It simply depended upon moderation,
good sense, and the exercise of what he called real
English qualities, to ensure success. He looked
upon this work with great satisfaction, because he
felt that in such an act as they . had done that day
they had, so to speak, knitted a fresh bond of
union between different classes. We lived in
times when there was very often a great deal of
misrepresentation on this subject. Good edgcation,
however, was much wider and broader spread than
formerly, and he had that confidence in it himself
that he believed that the more men were educated,
the more they looked into these questions, and the
, more they would be satisfied that other men of a
different class are not their enemies or ill-wishers,
but that it is in the inter* of all classes to live
together in an honest, friendly, and Christian
spirit.

The actors in the latest Hoxton tragedy,

Mr. Butt, M.P., addressed the trades of
Limerick on Tuesday night. Dealing with

not injure the rights of a single man. If

Irish people, then, indeed, another question
would arise.

articles.title: WARS, KINGS, AND PEOPLES.
articles.text:
WARS, KINGS, AND PEOPLES.

'Twat' man himself
Brought death into the world'; and man himself
Gave keenness to his darts, quicken'd his paco,
And multiplied destruction on mankind.
With joy Ambition saw, and soon improv'd
The execrable deed. 'Twos not enough
By subtle hand to snatch a single life
Puny impiety! whole kingdoms fell
To sate the lust of power; more horrid still,
The foulest stain and scandal of our nation,
Became its boast. One murder made a villain—
Millions a hero. Princes were privileged
To kill, and numbers sanctified the crime.
Ah ! why will kings forget that they are men?
And men that they are brethren ? Why delight
In human sacrifice? Why burst the ties
Of nature, that should unit their souls together
In one soft bond of amity and love?
Yet still they breed destruction, still go on
Inhumanly, ingenious to find out
New pains for life, new terrors for the grave.
Artificers of Death! Still monarchs dream
Of universal empire growing up
From universal ruin. Blast the design,
Great God of Hosts; nor let Thy creatures fill
Unpited victims at. Ambition's shrine.

The Dublin Express reports that an incident
which is of rare occurrence in Ireland, took
place in a Roman Catholic chapel in Dublin,
on Sunday,. A blooming country girl drove to
the chapel, attended by her friends, for the
purpose of getting married. The bridegroom
had arranged to meet the bridal party at the
chapel, but he did not keep his promise. The
bride waited for several hours, but no bride-
groom put in an appearance, and at length,
amid the sympathy of the male speotators, but
apparently to the satisfaction of the females
present, she re-entered the vehicle and drove
homewards.

At the County Magistrates' Court, Liverpool,
on Saturday, Richard Howard, recently em-
ployed, as an engine-driver on the Lancashire

endangering the lives of passengers on the line
by not obeying signals. On the 21st of
August the prisoner, while driving an engine
from Liverpool to Southport, ran into a train
at Seaforth, causing considerable damage and
seriously shaking many of the passengers.
He had kept close behind the train all the way
up to the time of the collision, although it was
said that the signals were against him. The
company, considering him to blame, discharged

contended that it was a common practice to
drive a light engine close behind, and that in
this particular case the defendant was signalled
by Rags, at the various stations he passed, to
go on. The prisoner was committed for trial,
bail being accepted.

On Saturday night an old woman named
Margaret Ward, about 70 years of age, was
brutally murdered at Sheffield by a labourer,
who is known as "Scotty Jack.' The parties
lodged at one of the lodging-houses in Water-
lane, which is a very disreputable neighbour-
hood. At seven o'clock the old woman was
sitting upon the doorstep smoking, "Scotty
Jack" being inside the house. A wordy battle
then took place on the subject of " Sootty's"
nationality. After some little time the man
lost his temper, used some disgusting language,
and ran at the old woman, whom he dealt a
heavy kick on the back of the neck. She fell
forward on the pavement, and when some
women lifted her up they found she was dead.
"Scotty Jack" was immediately apprehended,
but refuses to give his name. As he has only
been in Sheffield for about a week no one
knows anything regarding him.

The Registrar-General reports that the
average death. rate in the large towns of the
United Kingdom last week was 24 per 1,000.
Small-pox prevailed at Portsmouth, and scarlet
fever, with increased fatality, at Oldham. In
London' 2,070 births and 1,203 deaths were -
reported, being at the rate of 19 per 1,000.
The most serious zymotic diseases were 22
cases Of scarlet fever, 26 of hooping-cough,
29 of fever (chiefly typhoid), and 116 of
diarrhcea. There were 52 deaths from violence,
including three suicides and one manslaughter.
Only 3 people were killed in the street, but
54 were injured.

Lieut. Dawson has very properly retaliated
on the Royal Geographical Society for the
censure passed upon him in connoetion with
the Livingstone Relief Expedition. Fre charges
his judges with having distorted the facts of
the defence, and repeats in the strongest terms
his allegation which has been so rife of late
that Livingstone's professed friends wore least'
anxious about relieving him.

On Monday Superintendent Gregory, of the
Doncaster police force, presented to the justices
of that borough are port, stating that at the recent
races illegal gaming was entirely suppressed.
Special detectives had been employed, who
kept the strictest watch upon the suspected
saloons, but no infringement of the law was
reported.

Newgate has witnessed another edifying
performance with "the cat." Daniel Duffey,
a young ruffian of eighteen, who took a sailor
up a passage and robbed him bore his five-
and-twenty lashes very pitifully—writhing
and screaming all the while. The other sub-
ject, John Talbot, who had garrotted a
labourer near the Borough Afarka, took the
first of his punishment with mole bravado,
but at the fifth stroke he relented.

The Mayor of Norwich has received an
offloial 'communication from the Lord Chan-
cellor, through his lordship's secretary, in-
timating that he will give his anxious con-
sideration to the circumstances of the late
magisterial fracas at Norwich as soon as the
necessary documents have been laid before
him. These documents have since, it appears,
been submitted to the noble and learned lord
through the Home Secretary.

Alice Oswald's remains were followed to the
grave at Woking Cemetery by a number of
English and American ladies. The burial'
sumo was read by the Rev. Horace Roberts.
Subscriptions were collected at the grave to
defray the cost of the freehold, which has been
purchased by Miss Stride, and for the erection
of a memorial tombstone.

A correspondent writes that, having a
daughter at school in Auxerre, in France, he
sent her a small box containing a plain muslin
dress and that upon its arrival there 12 francs
were 'demanded and paid for duty. On his
writing to the general manager of the south-
Eastern Railway, he received in reply the
explanation that the charge referred to had
been levied in consequence of the alteration
made in the French customs duties, and that
the duty on dresses is now 15 per amt.

articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The judge charged with the preliminary,
inquiry into the case of M. About, at Stras-
burg, peremptorily refuses to allow the
prisoner to see anybody except his wife until
the inquiry is terminated, It is expected the
inquiry will last several days longer.
The Socialist leader, Dr. Hepner, editor of
Vothstaat, has been arrested by the Leipsio
police, for having attended the Inter-
national Congress at the Hague, the Leipsie
authorities having interdicted membership of
Socialist associations or congresses to all
persons resident within their j urisdiction.
The Yarmouth magistrates yesterday, at an
adjourned meeting, decided to extend the
hour of opening public-houses to five a.m.,
and also to allow such houses to remain open
until midnight for four mouths in the year, to
meet the requirements of visitors. The
publicans talk of calling a public meeting to
discuss the question.
The Earl of Jersey was married yesterday
to the Hon. Margaret Leigh, eldest 'laughter
of Lord Leigh of Stoneleigh Abbey, War-
wickshire. The ceremony took place at St.
Thomas's Church, Portman-square. Immo-
diatey after the opening of the doors, the
Church was orowded with fashionable specta-
tors. At the conclusion of the oeremony the
bridal party proceeded to Lord Leigh's resi-
dence in Portman-square. The Earl of Jersey
was born on the 20th of March, 1846, and Miss
Leigh (now Countess of Jersey) in 1849.
The snatch between the St. aeorge's Club;
New York, and the English Eleven was com-
menced on Wednesday, the St. George's
ecoring 66 runs in their first innings. The
English then sent in Messrs. Grace and Otto-
way; who stored 102 runs and were not out
When the stumps were drawn.
The Preston Guardian reports the death of
Lady Kay-Shuttleworth, the wife of Sir James
P. Kay-Shuttleworth, of aawthorpe Hall,
near Burnley.
A boatman named Eli Brett, of Horne Bay,
took a gentleman to Margate by boat. Late in
the evening Brett started on his return voyage
ond while in sight of Margate jetty, his boat,
Which was evidently top heavy with sails, Was
seen to tack about, and then suddenly go
down. Brett was soon picked up, but all
efforts to restore animation failed. He leaves
a wife and live or six children.
The premises of Mr. Coppers, oowkeeper
and dairyman, near the Waterloo-road, were
destroyed by are yesterday morning.

From New York we hear that Mr. Horace
Greeley has gone upon a tour to the West, and
everywhere large crowds assemble to meet
Mm. He frequently delivers speeches, iti
which he counbels reconciliation and the
abandonment of all party ties, declaring him-
self to be the candidate of universal amnesty.

An official letter has been addressed to Prince
Charles with reference to the arrest of the
Greek Vice-Consul at Ibraila. Assuming the
good intentions of the Prince, the Porto ex-
presses the hope that entire satisfaction will
be given to the parties interested, and that the
Roumanian authorities in future will not be
Wanting in respect for the firmans which the
Consuls receive from the Suzerain Court.
The Manchester Guardian states that the
wall of a mill was struck down by lightning,
on Wednesday evening at Littleborough
near Roolidale, and four women were killed.
Mr. Raffles, the Liverpool stipendiary, re-
ceived a threatening letter on Tuesday, stating
that he would be shot in court during the day.
Strict watch was accordingly kept, but nothing
unusual transpired.
Another railway collision took place on
'Wednesday morning. The first-class express
market train from Manchester to Bradford ran
into a goods train near Miles Platting. Some
half-dozen of the goods trucks were thrown.
one on the top of the other. The passenger's
in the express train escaped with slight in-
juries.

Mr. Charles Morgan, the farmer who was
brought up at Pontypool a week ago on the
charge of shooting three boys who had ven-
tured to take an apple from a tree in his
orchard, was again examined. His offer of
compensation, and an intimation from the
aggrieved parties that a money urrangement
would satisfy them, failed to meet with the
approval of the magistrates, who committed
Mr. Morgan for trial.
An inquest was held on Wednesday in
Bethnal-green on the body of Georginia Peel,
aged 38. The deceased lived near a Mrs.
Moon, with whom she had been on friendly
terms, A quarrel, however, unfortunately
took place, and Mrs. Moon struck the deeased
with such violence behind the left ear as to
cause instantaneous death. A verdict of
manslaughter was returned.
The death is announced of Sir William
Harrison Walker, senior professional member
of the Marine and Harbour Departments of
the Board of Trade. Sir William had. com-
pleted his seventy-second year,

THE AMA.LGAMATED SOCIETY OF
RAILWAY SERVANTS.
To the Editor of the BEE. HIVE.

SlR,—Sinco my last letter to the BEE-HIVE
many ominous signs have appeared—some in
distance, others very near—of the Amalga-
mated Society of Railway Servants becoming
split up into a number of small and, conse-
quently, useless parts,
I don't know that any branch has yet
actually decided, but I know for certain that
if things do not take a decided favourable
turn, several branches will immediately do so.
This is much to be deplored, the more so as it
might be avoided. Yes, Sir, might be avoided,
and wottld be I have no doubt, if a few of the
present ruling spirits had mere brains, even
more scrupulous and economical, and less
selfish.

This pessibility, or rather probability, of open
revolt, Sir, is to be attributed to a variety of
causes, one of which I alluded to in the latter
part of my former communication; but the
principal cause is that of the Executive
Council having imposed a levy of is. per
member, for the support of a strike with which
the Society had nothing whatever to do, in
fact, altogether disapprove of. A great many
branches have positively refused to pay this
levy; others have asked for time to consider
as to whether they shall do so or not, and I an'
personally acquainted with not a few individual
members who have declared that they will
have no more to do with the concern. They
contend that these North-Western men who
struck had not sufficient cause, and if they had,
they should have borne with it till after the wages
and hours question had been properly and
satisfactorily adj usted, and then have consulted
with and obtained the sanction of the Society
through its Executive Council before taking
any steps towards that end.
It seems to me) Sir, that as this was
not done, the Council has unwarrantably ex.
ceeded its powers.
These, Sir, ate some of' the reasons urged
against the payment of this levy i but not a
few are most woefully offended because some
of the leaders in this strike, and the authors
of several rash and, as Mr. Bass describes
them, " insane " speeches the advisers of
wild and wicked devices, and the propagators
of groundless charges of bribery against the
press) from whom the whole body has received
so much valuable support, are still allowed to
take part in the government of the Society.
That they have brought much discredit
upon the Society, is beyond a doubt;
and I have been trying to imagine the feelings
of those who think so when they come to
see the feelers which were thrown out in the
little pennyworth of last week, that some of these
eter-to-be.feared gentlemen should be sent
beyond the Tweed and across the Channel as
organizing secretaries to the society. It is to be
hoped that this will not be attempted, as if it
is, the axe, which is now at its full height,
will be brought down with sufficient force and
vengeance to sever three-fourths of the
branches from the parent stem. Moreover, it
will prove that what they told Mr. Vincent
about their financial position not allowing
them to employ him was false; indeed, I look
upon that as being proved already by having
engaged a clerk at 355. per week, paid their
president to go on a tour to the north, and
given .£3 each to the Furniture Committee 01
This latter part has taken my breath away.
I can make nothing of it, and therefore must
beg to remain respectfully yours,
A RAILWAY MAN.

MR. BRIGGS AND THE WEST YORK-

SHIRE MINERS' UNION.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Slit,—As a practical man, I will, with your
permission, place before your readers facts
which can be substantiated by evidence, and
not inferences and suppositions, which have no
existence only in the biassed mind of Mr.
Briggs. He says with respect to trade unions
—"I um not prepared to deny that the col-
liers have reaped some good therefrom." Now
it pleases me thread from Mr. Briggs' pen the
above admission, because I never before either
heard or read of him allowing that there was
any good whatever in trade organizations,
while I have many times heard of him con-
demning them as being ruinous both to men
and masters. He adds, further, however :
"But I am bold to assert that whatever may
be the advantageous results of colliers' unions,
the policy of such associations has often been
inimical to the real interests of their mem-
bers.' I will venture to say that Mr. Briggs,
after his ill-temper is allowed to cool down,
will he ready to admit that the benefits accruing
to labour from the influenoe of trade organiza-
tions have been real and practical, that the
results have not been inimical to their real
interests, but the improvements in their
position are both solid and laiting, They have

secured to the members more wages and mare
home comforts. The reasonings and dis-
cussions that have taken. place in their
committees and public meetings have
been the means of educating them in trade
matters, and the result of these discussions
are that the miners are more steady, less
headstrong, better servants, not so eager to
rush into strikes as they used to be, and I can
tall him—if he does not already know it—that
the interests of capital is not 'lost sight of at
these meetings; on the contrary, the position
and prospects of both masters and men are
carefully considered, and a spirit of concilia-
tion manifested in every instance. But he'
continues, "and the ruling spirit of their
councils has been, and continues to be, one of
antagonism to their masters." If he can find
me one single instance where the councils of
our association are antagonistic to the masters,
I will agree that there might be some reason
for saying so, but I challenge him to find one
single action, one resolution, one document, or
one word of advice given from our present
councils, that he or anyone else can construe
into a spirit of antagonism towards the masters
of this district. Nor would his assertion be
endorsed by a half-dozen colliery owners in
the West Riding of Yorkshire who had any
experience of trades unions. The spirit from
which such an assertion emanated is pregnant
with hatred of trade unions without being
tempered with either justice or Christian
charity. He says they have " been very
careful to avoid doing anything by word or
act, indirect or positive, in opposition to the
miners union of this district.' I fancy when
some of ,the miners saw this, they would ex-
claim in real collier's fashion, "Well, if ever."
It is not for me to say what he has done in the
past, nor what he may do in the future. I
can only say, that if he will deal fairly with
the men, the union will not try to injure either
him or hid scheme of industrial partnership.
He talks of forming a widow's fund, and
making the benevolent advantages equal to
the union in order that the men may leave
the union. I wonder he never thought of this
before during the whole six years the indus-
trial partnership has been carried on. There
has been both men and boys killed, and
women and children left destitute, besides men
being permanently injured, but no provision
for such has been made before now that a few
months since the men made provision for
themselves by joining the union. Now when
he sees that they are determined to go on
with the union, that they have already one
widow on the funds whose husband has been
killed at the works since they entered, and
that already more than £4O has been paid
for funeral purposes in a few months' time,
which causes them to appreciate and value
its benefits, he will try to subvert its action
by creating a rival fund at the collieries. Mr.
Briggs complains of the men saying they in-
tended to go to the demonstration at Leeds,
and he would lead us to infer that the word-
ing of this note was the chief cause of his pro-
hibiting them from going. I should think he
has known that the miners are not very
choice in their expressions, and that
the words intend to go were meant simply to
let him know they desired to go and obtain
his approval. He thinks it very wrong that
they should want to throw the pits idle on the
very day the annual meeting of the share-
holders was to take place. I would ask Mr.
Briggs to be faithful and tell your readers
whether or not it was he that caused the clash
by calling the shareholders' meeting on the
very day the demonstration took place. The
demonstration was arranged for on the 17th of
June, and arrangements were in active opera-
tion before Mr. Briggs called the shareholders'
meeting which had never been held so late
before nor had the bonus ever been paid so
late before, and I will tell your readers what
Mr. Briggs already knows, but did not like to
say in his letter, that the prevalent opinion.
here, both among his workmen and outsiders,
that he called the meeting on that particular
day, knowing that it would come in direct
contact with the demonstration, and would
form a pretext for him prohibiting their
attendance at Leeds. He refers to my circular
of appeal to him and says I called it a day of
pleasure. Yes, it a day of pleasure, and I
hope to see many more such days of pleasure,
and can tell Mr. Briggs such days and such
speeches as he styles union speeches will tend
to do more towards the improvement of the
miners, as a body, and even to capital than all
his scheming ever did or ever will. Mr. Briggs
concludes by saying that the body of workmen
employed at their collieries are amongst the
most industrious and intelligent in West
Yorkshire. I endorse this statement, and
when Mr. Briggs acknowledges this and finds
that after six years experience under the
practice of industrial partnerships these
intelligent men should still find the necessity
of union, I think he should not throw obstacles
in the way of their having one. I will con-
clude by asking him to forget the bitterness
of the past, and be assured that so long as Mr.
Briggs keeps those men who created this
bitterness under his wing, there will be no
more threatening letters wrote nor conspiracies
entered into for the purpose of destroying pro-
perty.—Yours,
liormanton.

L Dins.

SEPT. 21, 1872.

STANDING ARMIES.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

_
Sr,—lfr. Latham's "Root Questions seem
to have stirred up some critics, who appear to.
fear that" peace at any price" is the "root "
policy. I confess that I did not so read the
articles, referred to, but consider them as
setting forth the utter absurdity of the present
system of maintaining great and expensive
military establishments, doubtless no fault of
the country alone, bat one in which she has to
share the blame with others. However, to
give a practical character to this question Of
standing armies, allow me to suggest that the,
matter may be viewed in two ways.
Ist. As to whether it is absolutely necessary
for the preservation of peace that standing'
armies should exist
2nd. That in endeavouring to substitute
peaceful settlements for warfare, is it dr
sirable that this country should do is it did in
the case of Free Trade—set a good example to
other nations?

As to the first point, the necessity for a
large standing army is to my mind a mistake.
For the defence of a country in whioh pa'
triotism extensively prevails, as it does
this, an arm-trained population is far superior
to any standing army of professional soldiers
of such numerical strength as we are ever
likely to agree to maintain. For let us sup-
pose that some enemy invades the country,
and is opposed, as he would be in his first
onslaught, by our comparatively small stand-
ing army, that body, or a large proportion of
it, would probably be soon placed hors do
combat, for no sane enemy would attempt a
descent upon us without having provided him-
self with such overwhelming means of attack as
to enable him to establish a footing on our
soil. After our standing army had thus been
broken up, unless we capitulated, we should
have to fall back upon our armed populatien,
and the real hard fighting would thus remain
to be done by them. This view of the case
shows that after all the great expense we arc
at in maintaining our army, it would, in effect,
prove itself to be nothing better than a reliance.
on a broken reed in the hour of trial. As to
our being able, relying upon our standing
army, to carry on a foreign aggressive war, if
the matter were not one of such sobering and
saddening character, the thought would be
laughable, as the 40,000 or 60,000 men we
could manage to send to the war would soon be
disposed of, and then how should we supply
their places?
It seems to me, therefore, that what we
want is an arm-trained population in lieu of
an army; something like the Swiss military
system, and unlike the Prussian system,
which our rulers seem just now so much
enamoured with. No doubt we should require
a central corps of highly trained men and
officers; but the old plan of trained-bands,:
organized in and for each county, and kept up
at its expense, should be the system adopted,
for I hold, in accordance with the views of Mr.
Lai ham, that armed-men, placed at the abso-
lute control of the Central Governments, i*.
dangerous to public liberty, and here I cannot
refrain from remarking that it was a step
in a downward direction when Mx. Cardwel,
by his own army scheme, took the militia out
of the power of the counties. The Central
Governments could usefully occupy itself with
training efficient officers, and taking care that
some others should be employed, and that each
&may kept up its quota of men, but ought
not to be allowed to do more than this. to
my mind their maintenance.of standing armies
means repression of democratic; power and the
keeping up of the military profession. I, for
one, have no sympathy with either of these
objects • and I feel sure that otherwise, in-
stead of occupying ourselves with marchings,
and countermarchings, and other Autuma
Manceuvre-displays ; we should turn our at-
tention to guarding ourselves by means og
soientifie engines of warfare, in opposing
which an enemy would recoil with horror.
As regards my second point, I say, let
England take the lead, bt declaring it to be
her future policy to adopt International Arbi-
tration rather than war.
Before concluding, however, allow me to
make one remark on Mr. William H. Laird'il
notion, that the money spent in keeping metlf
at work in an unproductive industry is an
good to the nation? Surely, whether as
matter of political economy or humanity, this
must be wrong.-1 ours truly,
F. W. CLIIPIS.

of Mr. Joseph Johnson, who some 50 years ago
was an active associate of Hunt, Cobbett, and
Bamford, and underwent two years' imprison-
ment as one of the leaders at Peterloo.
refused, however, to take part in a reform
demonstration some ten years afterwards, al
was a Tory sui generis during the last half
his long life.

According to some statistical returns which
have been issued by the Board of Trade, the
number of acres of land under wheat in Great
Britain in the present year is 3,599,158; of
barley, 2,316,235; of oats, 2,706,645; of

contract --hris been concluded between -th
Spanish Government and the Banque de Pani
for the conversion of the Spanish debt, and
the reduction of the rate of interest.

According to the report of the Agricultural
Department the cotton crop in the United
States will be 10 per cent. below the average)
though probably in excess of that of last year,

A young man who had created a disturbance
in the South London Musics Hall, and assaulted
one of the officials, has been sentenced by the
Southwark police magistrate to six weeks'
imprisonment with hard labour.

An auxiliary letter-carrier, in the service of
,the Post-office, was on Wednesday committed
for trial from the Thames Police-court, on a
charge of having illegally opened and detained
letters entrusted to him for delivery.

On Wednesday the tank of England raised
the rate of discount from 3i to 4 per cent.
The course taken by the directors, in raising
the rate within 24 hours of their usual weekly
• meeting, attrabted considerable attention.

A confidential clerk, in a largo public com-
pany in Cork, is reported to have absconded
with a sum of over £2,000, which- had been
entrusted to him to draw 'a letter of credit in
favour of a manufacturing firm in England.

ballot was held on Wednesday, a member of
the Town Council being elected for St.
Thomas's Ward. There were two candidates
—Mr. J. E. Baker, Liberal, a supporter of the
policy of the National Education League; and
3,1 r. T. Parkes, a Conservative, an opponent of
the Licensing Act, and a supporter of denomi-
national 'ed.bdatiOn. The election was Ilia&
on these two points—the Licensing Act and
religious teaching in rate-aided schools. The
constituency of tha ward is 5,700, and of
these Inirdly: a third voted. The election
passed off quietly, and resulted in the return
of Mr. Baker by a majority of 336. The cry.
Of "The Bible in schools" had been freely used,
and the defeat of the clerical party is oo nsi
dered an event of much local signifioance.

On Tuesday evening large numbers of
students of Newton Abbot College were waiting
on the platform of the Dawlish Railway
Station for the down train. On its arrival,
and before it had stopped, several of them
rushed for the carriages, and one, named
Brooking, son of a gentleman who only last
week sailed for India fell between the train
and the platform, and two carriages passed
over both his legs, crushing them dreadfully,
A large number of persons were on the plat-
form, and the accident created great con-
sternation. The poor lad, who bore the pain
with extraordinary fortitude, was removed to
the adjoining hotel, where one leg was ampu-
tated. No blame is attached to any one,
